title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: all the gods gather before the goddess and ask her the plainest question there is: who are you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakti as a philosophy through Samkhya's dancer: prakriti shows herself to the watcher, and once she's been fully seen, she stops. Did a strong feeling walk off on its own? Day one thousand eighty-seven.

Who are you? It's the question you ask a stranger at the door, a new neighbor, a voice on the phone. In a short text called the Devi Upanishad, it's the question every god asks the goddess. They come and stand before her, all of them together, and ask: who are you, great goddess? Yesterday, in Samkhya, nature danced and said nothing. She was watched, and then she left. Today she is asked to speak for herself. And the answer she gives is not a name, or a family, or a list of victories. Today: the goddess, asked who she is, in her own words.
screen: `ALL THE GODS COME TO HER.` → `WHO ARE YOU, GREAT GODDESS?` → `TODAY SHE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's her answer, in paraphrase. I am of the very nature of Brahman. From me comes this world, made of prakriti and purusha, nature and spirit, the empty and the not-empty. I am joy and not-joy. I am knowing and not-knowing. Turn it the first way: she answers with Brahman. The ultimate reality, the one Uma named for Indra in the Kena: here the goddess simply says, that's me. Second, look at the pair she claims. Prakriti and purusha. Yesterday Samkhya kept them as two: the dancer and the watcher, never the same. Here both come from her. The goddess isn't only the dancer anymore. She is the dance and the one watching it. In this text, power is not one half of reality. It is the whole, seen from the side that moves and gives. Third, the pairs of opposites. Empty and not-empty, joy and not-joy, knowing and not-knowing. She doesn't pick the comfortable half. She claims both. In this text's picture, the gentle and the rough both sit inside her, not outside. Fourth, what the gods do next. The text has them bow and praise her. It's a whole movement in a few lines: a question, an answer that is bigger than the question, and then worship. Not everyone on the Hindu path reads it this way; Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions name the highest reality Vishnu or Shiva. In this Upanishad, the goddess answers for herself.
screen: `I AM OF THE NATURE OF BRAHMAN.` · `PRAKRITI AND PURUSHA, BOTH FROM HER.` · `EMPTY AND NOT-EMPTY. JOY AND NOT-JOY.` · `THE GODS BOW, AND PRAISE HER.` · then, large: `WHO ARE YOU? I AM BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: both halves. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice one comfortable thing right now: warmth, a soft seat, a quiet room. Hold it for a few breaths. Then notice one uncomfortable thing: a tight shoulder, a worry, a noise you'd rather not hear. Hold that too, without pushing it away. Then let both sit in the same space, side by side, the way the goddess holds joy and not-joy. If you pray, you can rest in the name of the Devi, or the name you use for God. If you don't, rest in the space that holds both. The bell holds the time.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Devi Upanishad, the gods ask who she is, and she answers: of the nature of Brahman, the source of prakriti and purusha both.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Today, ask someone you think you know well a real who-are-you question, and listen to the whole answer. Day one thousand eighty-seven.

howItsDone: The Devi Upanishad, also called the Devi Atharvashirsha, is chanted by worshippers of the goddess, including during Navaratri, and is studied as a statement of the goddess as ultimate reality.

fork.setup: you're the goddess. all the gods stand before you and ask: who are you? what do you say?
options: I am the wife of Shiva.
I am of the nature of Brahman; from me comes the world.
I am the strongest of the gods.
fork.reveal: she says she is of the very nature of Brahman, and that the world of prakriti and purusha comes from her. then the gods bow and praise her.

original.note: Sanskrit: brahmasvarupini, she whose very form is Brahman: the goddess's answer in the Devi Upanishad.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shakti is one half of God.
what it means: in the Devi Upanishad she is the whole: Brahman, and the source of nature and spirit both.
what a scholar hears: sābravīd ahaṃ brahmasvarūpiṇī, mattaḥ prakṛtipuruṣātmakaṃ jagat: she reframes Samkhya's two inside one goddess.

notes: Devi Upanishad 1–2 paraphrased: sarve vai devā devīm upatasthuḥ, kāsi tvaṃ mahādevīti; sābravīt ahaṃ brahmasvarūpiṇī, mattaḥ prakṛtipuruṣātmakaṃ jagat, śūnyaṃ cāśūnyaṃ ca; aham ānandānānandau, ahaṃ vijñānāvijñāne. Verse numbering differs by edition; confirm. 'Then the gods bow and praise her' follows the namo devyai stanzas that come after; confirm.
The sentence 'Vaishnava and Shaiva teachers place the highest reality in Vishnu or in Shiva' names differences without ranking; Keeper to check fairness.
